title: STM32: SPI.read(n) fails if n > 1 (regression)
body:
This arose driving an EEPROM using hard SPI on Pyboard D hardware (soft SPI works OK). Baudrate was 5MHz, other args default. Hardware is a Pyboard D on a DIP28 adaptor on a small PCB with a pair of EEPROM chips on the bus. Traces are very short. This setup has worked in the past when developing [this driver](https://github.com/reporter/micropython_eeprom/blob/master/eeprom/spi/SPI.md), and in fact still works with a Pyboard D SF2W running
```
MicroPython v1.18-355-g9ab66b50c-dirty on 2022-04-29; PYBD-SF2W with STM32F722IEK
```
With a Pyboard D SF6W running
```
MicroPython v1.22.1 on 2024-01-05; PYBD-SF6W with STM32F767IIK
```
it behaves as follows. A single byte read from an arbitrary address returns the correct contents, but a multi-byte read returns a bytes object of the correct length but containing zeros. To investigate the fault reading was done with a simple `spi.read(n)`. The hardware was examined with an LA: the single byte and multi-byte reads were identical aside from the extra byte and conformed with the device spec. The MISO result for a 2-byte read was as follows:
![Image](https://github.com/reporter/micropython-samples/blob/master/temp/read_2_hard.jpg?raw=true)

The LA shows correct data being transmitted by the EEPROM but `spi.read(2)` returned `b'\x00\x00'`.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: I can't claim to fully grasp the code, but [this line](https://github.com/micropython/micropython/blob/16c6bc47cf2b9247418bca8c0d1361167d08594e/ports/stm32/spi.c#L603) does indicate that multi-byte transfers use DMA, while single byte ones do not. Not a smoking gun, perhaps, but maybe a dripping water pistol...

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
From what you've shown it can probably be tested on a standalone pybd with a miso pin simply tied high, should return 1's when working, 0's on failure.
It does sound like it could be a mixup / overlap of dma channel configs; these are  separate for each stm chip family which would explain why it's not seen on _all_ stm boards.
Also, the onboard SPI flash chips are used softspi and hard qspi, again explaining why it's not seen there.

Is it straightforward for you to test on some more versions, get a closer idea of when the issue came in?

comments.body:
Unfortunately tying the pin high does not demonstrate the failure. I also tried linking `MOSI` and `MISO` and running the following:
```python
from machine import Pin, SoftSPI, SPI
```

This also failed to demonstrate the issue.

I'd welcome any suggestion how I might be making a mistake here, but as far as I can see the LA trace is textbook correct. It has me completely foxed: I can't see why single byte transfers work and multi byte ones fail; or why hard SPI has problems while soft SPI works with transfers of any length. The latter has been extensively tested.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
The top trace on the LA is `CS\`. All LA signals are identical with single and multi byte transfers except for the extra clock pulses and MISO data as shown.

I checked for the notion that pins are being reconfigured under working and failing firmware builds.
```
Working firmware 1.18
>>> from machine import Pin
>>> Pin('Y6')
Pin(Pin.cpu.B13, mode=Pin.ALT, pull=Pin.PULL_DOWN, af=Pin.AF5_SPI2)
>>> Pin('Y7')
Pin(Pin.cpu.C2, mode=Pin.ALT, pull=Pin.PULL_DOWN, af=Pin.AF5_SPI2)
>>> Pin('Y8')
Pin(Pin.cpu.C3, mode=Pin.ALT, pull=Pin.PULL_DOWN, af=Pin.AF5_SPI2)
>>> 
Current firmware 1.22.1
>>> Pin('Y6')
Pin(Pin.cpu.B13, mode=Pin.ALT, pull=Pin.PULL_DOWN, alt=Pin.AF5_SPI2)
>>> Pin('Y7')
Pin(Pin.cpu.C2, mode=Pin.ALT, pull=Pin.PULL_DOWN, alt=Pin.AF5_SPI2)
>>> Pin('Y8')
Pin(Pin.cpu.C3, mode=Pin.ALT, pull=Pin.PULL_DOWN, alt=Pin.AF5_SPI2)
``` 
To put this into context I was reluctant to raise this issue especially as the loopback test passed. I therefore went to lengths to be sure there wasn't a silly mistake on my part swapping hardware - even assembling a new PCB - and checking signals with a scope (they look fine). The code is a simple test of the [EEPROM library](https://github.com/reporter/micropython_eeprom/blob/master/eeprom/spi/SPI.md). This was developed with hard SPI some years ago. It stopped working after a firmware upgrade.

The following observations seem pertinent.

It works fine with no other change if `HARD` is set to `False`:
```python
            if HARD:
                spi = SPI(2, baudrate=5_000_000)
            else:
                spi = SoftSPI(baudrate=5_000_000, sck=Pin("Y6"), miso=Pin("Y7"), mosi=Pin("Y8"))
```
Observations about the firmware:
1. The firmware handles single transfers without using DMA; single transfers always work.
2. There were changes to the DMA code at the time where the firmware starts to fail.

I'm struggling to see how this can be other than a firmware issue - but I'm as baffled as you by the loopback and "tied high" tests.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
@participant2 Thanks for confirming, but I can't confirm your baudrate observation. The above LA trace shows 9 cycles in 2μs which is close to 5MHz.

I am getting more odd results with hard SPI. With the aim of creating a reproducer I wired up a 74LS73 JK with `clk` connected to `sck` and `Q` connected to `MISO`. `clr\` was connected to pin Y4. The aim was to produce the same 0x55 data as in the above LA trace. I tested with the following.
```python
from machine import SPI, Pin
rst = Pin("Y4", Pin.OUT)
spi = SPI(2, baudrate=5_000_000)
spi.write(b'\x06')
spi.write(b'\x02\0\0\0\0')  # Emulate EEPROM setup
rst(0)
rst(1)  # Reset the JK
spi.read(20)  # b'UUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUU' i.e. good (0x55).
```
The writes have no effect (`MOSI` is unconnected) but I wanted to replicate the same SPI commands as in the driver. The test did not reproduce the fault. I unplugged the Pyboard and plugged it into my EEPROM test rig and it failed. This makes no sense to me.

I then created a build from current source, fully expecting the failure to occur. Yet it worked.

I've just about run out of ideas. The totally consistent takeaways are:
1. Firmware <= 1.18 works.
2. Soft SPI works.
3. Single byte reads (and all writes) work.

I am convinced that there is some kind of marginal condition with hard SPI multi-byte reads, but finding a guaranteed repro is proving to be beyond me.

comments.author: participant2
reporter
comments.body:
@participant2 Good find.

I replaced instances of multi-byte reads with `spi.write_readinto()` **with different buffers** and the driver now works with hard SPI on STM32 running latest firmware.

comments.body: Good. But that should only be a temporary patch.

2. Linking MOSI and MISO.
3. Toggling MISO.

It is a remarkably elusive bug.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
I changed the Makefile, building the DMA driver with the option -O2.
```
# Don't use -Os for this file, because it causes DMA to fail sometimes for a F7 MPU
# if src and dest in memory are identical. May apply to other MCU's as well.
ifeq ($(MCU_SERIES), f7)
$(BUILD)/lib/stm32lib/STM32$(MCU_SERIES_UPPER)xx_HAL_Driver/Src/stm32$(MCU_SERIES)xx_hal_dma.o: COPT += -O2
endif
```
With that change SPI at the PYBD_SF6 works. It may be useful for other fast MCU's as well.

After two days break, I looked again at the topic and repeated the delay test. Adding a short delay before the first call to HAL_DMA_Start_IT() after line 1808 in stm32f7xx_hal_spi.c works now. The same happens if I insert that delay at the begin of HAL_DMA_Start_IT(). Even HAL_Delay(0) seems sufficient, reducing the delay to upmost three function calls, one assignment and one compare.
Strange! But that complies with the observation, that changing the optimization for either stm32f7xx_hal_spi.c or stm32f7xx_dma_spi.c worked.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
There may be no "smoking gun" bit of assembly for this root cause, due to speculative reads! [From the Cortex-M7 TRM chapter on speculative accesses](https://<redacted-host>/documentation/ddi0489/f/memory-system/speculative-accesses):

> Speculative cache linefills can be initiated to any Cacheable memory address, and in rare cases, regardless of whether there is any instruction that causes the cache linefill.

This likely explains why changing the optimisation level around related code worked around the issue.
